title: Cyberculture
description:
Commissioned by the Council of Europe as a report on the state of cyberspace, Cyberculture treats the network as a cultural form rather than a set of machines.

Lévy first describes the infrastructure and applications of cyberspace, then turns to what they imply for society. He takes up the art forms emerging online, the changing relation between people and knowledge, education, the preservation of culture, the growth of what he calls collective intelligence, the risk of exclusion, and the effects of the network on democracy and on city life. His argument is that the technology can widen democratic participation by drawing in more individuals and more groups. The book appeared in French from Éditions Odile Jacob in 1997; this English edition, translated by Robert Bononno, is volume 4 of the University of Minnesota Press series Electronic Mediations.

Lévy is a French theorist of digital culture. He had already published Les technologies de l'intelligence (1990), L'intelligence collective (1994, translated as Collective Intelligence in 1997) and Qu'est-ce que le virtuel? (1995), and he continued the argument afterwards in Cyberdémocratie (2002) and The Semantic Sphere (2011).
tags: Media Theory, Internet, Digital Culture, Collective Intelligence

title: Multimedia: From Wagner to Virtual Reality
description:
A reader that builds the history of digital multimedia out of its own source documents, running from Wagner's total artwork to virtual reality.

Randall Packer and Ken Jordan assemble primary texts by scientists including Vannevar Bush, Norbert Wiener and Douglas Engelbart alongside artists including John Cage, Nam June Paik and William Gibson, and set each within the exchange between the arts and the sciences that produced it. Editorial introductions supply the context for the interfaces, links and interactive forms that later became ordinary. William Gibson contributed the foreword, recommending the book with an earnestness he says he has seldom felt for a collection of historic texts. W. W. Norton published this first edition in 2001 at xxi and 394 pages; an expanded paperback followed in December 2002, collated at xxxviii and 458 pages and carrying a coda by Laurie Anderson.

Packer is a media artist and, at the time of publication, professor of electronic arts at the Maryland Institute College of Art in Baltimore. Jordan built early web publications including SonicNet, Word and MediaChannel, and works in New York.

title: You Are Not a Gadget: A Manifesto
description:
A computer scientist's case against the design assumptions of the social web, written by one of the people who built its precursors.

Lanier's subject is lock-in: the programming choices made at the birth of digital media that hardened into permanent conditions before anyone weighed them, among them the way software fixes what a user's identity can be. He follows those decisions into social networks, cloud storage and the Web 2.0 designs that put the aggregate output of crowds and algorithms above what individual people think, and asks what a future built on the same philosophy would produce. Alfred A. Knopf published it in January 2010; Vintage issued the paperback in February 2011.

Lanier is a computer scientist and musician who helped found the field of virtual reality, and has worked at the boundary between computer science and medicine, physics and neuroscience. He returned to the economics of networked culture in Who Owns the Future? He lives in Berkeley, California.

title: Dawn of the New Everything: Encounters with Reality and Virtual Reality
description:
Jaron Lanier's account of the invention of virtual reality, told as autobiography, technical history and philosophy at once.

The book follows Lanier from a childhood in New Mexico to the founding of his first company, and runs that life alongside a continuing argument about what virtual reality is for. Library cataloguers file it under three headings at once: computer-science biography, the philosophy of virtual reality, and its social effects. Henry Holt published it in November 2017 in 368 pages, with bibliographical references and an index. The Economist, The Wall Street Journal and Vox each named it one of the best books of the year.

Lanier is a computer scientist and musician who worked on virtual reality from the 1980s onward, and his publisher calls him the father of the field. His earlier books, among them You Are Not a Gadget, are arguments against what networked computing has done to people. Dawn of the New Everything turns the other way and makes the case that virtual reality can enlarge experience rather than flatten it.

title: Hatching Twitter: A True Story of Money, Power, Friendship, and Betrayal
description:
Nick Bilton's reported account of how Twitter was built and how its four founders fell out, published two days before the company's stock market debut in November 2013.

The book follows Evan Williams, Jack Dorsey, Biz Stone and Noah Glass through Twitter's first years. Money, credit and control were all in dispute, and so was the question of who had founded the company at all. Bilton worked from hundreds of interviews, documents and internal e-mails. He has said the reporting overturned the premise he first sold his publisher, which cast Dorsey as a sole founder unjustly pushed out. Reviewers mostly granted the sourcing and argued about the balance. Hannah Kuchler wrote in the Financial Times that the book tips too far toward Williams. The San Francisco Chronicle faulted it for tracking every personal quarrel while leaving the business story thin. Maud Newton, in the New York Times Book Review, called it fast-paced and perceptive.

Bilton wrote the book as a New York Times technology columnist and reporter in the paper's San Francisco bureau. He later became a special correspondent for Vanity Fair. Hatching Twitter reached the New York Times business bestseller list in December 2013, and Lionsgate optioned it for television development.

title: Twitter and Tear Gas: The Power and Fragility of Networked Protest
description:
The sociologist Zeynep Tufekci's account of how the internet changed protest, drawn from a decade inside the movements it describes, from Tahrir Square to Occupy to Gezi Park.

Her argument is that a networked movement can reach in days the scale the civil rights movement needed years to build, and that the shortcut has a cost. The 1963 March on Washington was the product of months of organising, and that work left behind an organisation able to make decisions and negotiate. A hashtag can fill a square without producing either, so the new movements stall at the moment a state adapts to them. Tufekci calls this the tactical freeze. She traces it through the Zapatistas' early use of the internet, the medical supply lines run over Twitter during the Arab Spring, Occupy's human microphone, and the tear gas in Istanbul in 2013, where she was present. Later chapters follow the governments' reply: flood the channel with confusion rather than censor it. Yale published the book in May 2017 and released the full text free online under a Creative Commons licence.

Tufekci grew up in Istanbul in the years after the 1980 military coup, worked as a programmer before turning to sociology, and taught at the University of North Carolina when the book appeared. She has since moved to Princeton and writes an opinion column for The New York Times. This is her first book.
tags: Media Theory, Social Media, Protest Movements, Internet, Political Sociology

title: Visual Studies: A Skeptical Introduction
description:
A critical introduction to visual studies that describes the field and then argues that it should look at more than it does.

Elkins first gives a road map of the field, setting out its major concerns and its principal theoretical sources. He then turns to what the field leaves out: why look only at the same handful of theorists, and why exclude non-Western art or the wealth of scientific images? The chapters are “What is Visual Studies?”, “The Subjects of Visual Studies”, “Ten Ways to Make Visual Studies More Difficult” and “What is Visual Literacy?”, followed by a short envoi. Routledge published it in 2003, with 40 black-and-white illustrations.

Elkins is Professor of Art History at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. His other Routledge titles include Stories of Art, How to Use Your Eyes, Pictures and Tears and What Painting Is, and this book is the one in which he turns his attention to the discipline of image study itself.

title: Nonhuman Photography
description:
A new philosophy of photography that considers imaging practices from which the human is absent, and argues that photography is nonhuman even when people make the pictures.

Zylinska starts from CCTV, drones, medical body scans and satellite images, where photography is decoupled from human agency and human vision. She argues that images made by artists and amateurs also contain a mechanical element. They run on technical and cultural algorithms that shape our cameras and our viewing habits. The book looks at what digitization does to established notions of art, culture and the media. It proposes that photography is a light-induced process of fossilization across media and time scales. It includes images from her own project, Active Perceptual Systems. MIT Press published it in 2017.

Zylinska is Professor of Media Philosophy and Critical Digital Practice at King's College London, and before 2021 taught at Goldsmiths. She combines writing with an image-making practice. Her later books include AI Art: Machine Visions and Warped Dreams (2020) and The Perception Machine (2023).
tags: Photography Theory, Nonhuman, Media Philosophy, Digital Media, Machine Vision

title: The Electric Meme: A New Theory of How We Think
description:
A 2002 monograph by the anthropologist Robert Aunger. It treats the meme as a physical object, a pattern of electrical charge in the brain, and not as a figure of speech.

Aunger describes memes as patterns that reproduce rapidly in a node of the brain, and uses that account to look at free will, human identity, consciousness and society. Free Press published it in New York with 392 pages, a bibliography and an index. The Library of Congress files it under memetics, social perception, and thought and thinking.

Aunger is a biological anthropologist and senior lecturer in evolutionary public health at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine. He has taught at the University of Chicago, Northwestern, Cambridge and University College London. He edited Darwinizing Culture: The Status of Memetics as a Science and wrote Gaining Control: How Human Behavior Evolved with Valerie Curtis.
tags: Memetics, Cultural Evolution, Cognition, Consciousness, Media Theory
notes: Free Press hardcover, 2002. A later paperback exists (ISBN 9781451612950, 2010). The publisher link goes to the Open Library record. Identified from a spine photograph; edition not checked against the copy. Subjects (LOC): Social perception; Memetics; Thought and thinking.

title: The Meme Machine
description:
Susan Blackmore's 1999 book argues that memes, the units of imitated culture, are replicators that evolve apart from genes, and that memetics deserves recognition as a science.

Richard Dawkins, who introduced the term in The Selfish Gene, wrote the foreword. Blackmore holds that a universal replicator needs fidelity, a high rate of reproduction and longevity, and that memes meet all three. She suggests memes may have driven the genetic evolution of the large human brain, and applies the idea to language, sexuality, the internet and the sense of self. Oxford University Press published it in 1999 with 264 pages.

Blackmore is a British writer, lecturer and skeptic, born in 1951, who earned a PhD in parapsychology at the University of Surrey and moved from belief in the paranormal to scientific doubt. She taught at the University of the West of England until 2001 and later wrote Consciousness: An Introduction and Conversations on Consciousness.

title: The Age of the Image: Redefining Literacy in a World of Screens
description:
A 2013 argument that the spread of video and screens has outrun our ability to read and make images, and that visual literacy should be taught as writing is.

Apkon compares recent changes in video recording, editing and distribution to the arrival of movable type. He says most people cannot read the grammar of visual communication or the craft of making it. He draws parallels between film grammar and written language and uses examples such as the 1960 Kennedy-Nixon debates to show how visuals shape perception. Martin Scorsese wrote the foreword. Farrar, Straus and Giroux published it in 2013, with 263 pages and a bibliography.

Apkon is a former Goldman Sachs investment banker with a Harvard MBA. He founded the Jacob Burns Film Center in Westchester, New York, in 2000, with visual literacy education at its center, and led it until 2013. He later directed the documentaries Disturbing the Peace (2016) and There Is Another Way (2025).

title: Iconophages: A History of Ingesting Images
description:
A history of the European and Mediterranean habit of eating images, from swallowed frescoes and icons to stamped eucharistic wafers and sculpted marzipan figures.

Koering follows iconophagy from ancient Egypt through the twentieth century and asks what religious, therapeutic and symbolic work people expected an ingested image to do. He draws on art history, anthropology, philosophy and the history of the body and the senses. The book runs to 480 pages with 120 black-and-white illustrations and was translated from the French by Nicholas Huckle.

Koering is professor of early modern art history at the University of Fribourg. His earlier books include Le Prince en représentation, on the decoration of the ducal palace at Mantua, and Caravage, juste un détail. Zone Books published Iconophages in 2024, and it was named a New York Times Best Art Book of the year.
tags: Media Theory, Art History, Image Theory, Anthropology, Religious Imagery

title: The Logic of Images: Essays and Conversations
description:
A collection of essays and conversations in which the film director Wim Wenders writes about his own films, in Michael Hofmann's English translation.

The book gathers eighteen short critical pieces on film, most of them from the 1980s and most concerned with Wenders's own work. The films discussed include The Scarlet Letter, The American Friend, Kings of the Road, Tokyo-Ga, Paris, Texas and Wings of Desire. The German original, Die Logik der Bilder: Essays und Gespräche, came out from Verlag der Autoren in 1988. Faber and Faber issued Hofmann's translation in London in 1991.

Wenders was born in Düsseldorf in 1945 and studied at the film school in Munich from 1967. In 1971 he co-founded the Filmverlag der Autoren with other directors. Paris, Texas (1984) won the Palme d'Or at Cannes, and he took the Best Director prize there for Wings of Desire (1987). Since the early 1980s he has also kept up a photographic project, Pictures from the Surface of the Earth, of desolate landscapes.

title: Black Meme: A History of the Images That Make Us
description:
A history of the meme as a form of Black visual culture, running from 1900 to the present and arguing that internet virality rests on Black life and Black death.

Legacy Russell works through archival and contemporary media. Her cases include the circulation of lynching postcards, Jet magazine's publication of the open-casket photograph of Emmett Till, television coverage of the protesters at Selma, the Rodney King video often called the first viral video, the Anita Hill hearings, and Lavish “Diamond” Reynolds's Facebook Live recording after Philando Castile was killed by police. She contends that digital culture would not exist in its current form without the contributions of Black people, and she also looks at positive depictions of Blackness in the media. The book was shortlisted for the NBCC Award for Criticism.

Legacy Russell is Executive Director and Chief Curator of The Kitchen in New York, the first Black person to hold the post since the organization's founding in 1971. From 2018 to 2021 she was Associate Curator of Exhibitions at the Studio Museum in Harlem. Her earlier book, Glitch Feminism: A Manifesto (Verso, 2020), develops a term she coined in 2012 for error as a resistance to the gender binary. Black Meme was also published by Verso, in 2024.

title: Crime Scenery in Postwar Film and Photography
description:
A 2019 monograph by Henrik Gustafsson on how film and photography treat crime scenes and the places left behind by violence after the Second World War.

The book follows a lasting tendency in postwar art to look at places emptied of people after violent encounters. It maps the afterlife of landscape in search of the political and ethical agency of the image, setting landscape studies beside Walter Benjamin and Georges Didi-Huberman on memory, trauma and secondary witnessing. Its sites include Beirut, the West Bank, postwar Germany and Poland. Palgrave Macmillan issued it in 2019 in hardcover with 285 pages, colour illustrations and an index.

Gustafsson is professor of media and documentation science at UiT The Arctic University of Norway, in Tromsø. His research covers postwar cinema and photography, memory, and the ethics of spectatorship. He co-edited Cinema and Agamben: Ethics, Biopolitics and the Moving Image (2014) and Gestures of Seeing in Film, Video and Drawing (2017).
tags: Film Studies, Photography, Landscape, Visual Culture, War and Memory

title: Image Factories: Infographics 1920–1945
editor: Helena Doudova, Stephanie Jacobs, Patrick Rössler
contributors: Bernd Stiegler (Essay); Otto Neurath (Author); Fritz Kahn (Author)
description:
The book examines the infographics of Fritz Kahn and Otto Neurath, two figures who worked on the visual presentation of information in the decades between the wars.

It accompanies Transformer: On Infographics as Media of Modernity, shown at the German Museum of Books and Writing in the German National Library, Leipzig, from 8 September 2017 to 7 January 2018. Historical material and imagery from 1920 to 1945 appear alongside contemporary infographics, with essays by Stephanie Jacobs, Patrick Rössler, Helena Doudova and Bernd Stiegler, and a text by Neurath. It has 176 pages with 80 black-and-white and 40 colour illustrations, thread-sewn, in English, designed by Kay Bachmann.

Helena Doudova, Stephanie Jacobs and Patrick Rössler edited the volume. Spector Books also issued a German edition, Bildfabriken: Infografik 1920–1945, and lists this English edition as out of print.

title: Program or Be Programmed: Ten Commands for a Digital Age
description:
A short polemic that treats programming as the literacy of the digital age and asks whether people direct their technology or are directed by it.

Rushkoff builds the argument as ten commands. He compares the shift to digital media with earlier ones. When people gained language they learned to speak as well as listen, and when they gained literacy they learned to write as well as read. The book holds that using programs without knowing how they are made gives up control to those who do. Understanding code, it says, gives access to the control panel of civilization. The 2010 OR Books paperback carries original illustrations by Leland Purvis.

Rushkoff writes on media, technology and society. A second edition from OR Books in 2024, Program or Be Programmed: Eleven Commands for the AI Future, adds a section on artificial intelligence.
tags: Media Theory, Digital Literacy, Programming, Technology and Society, Internet Culture

title: Posthuman Knowledge and the Critical Posthumanities
description:
A lecture by Rosi Braidotti, printed as a short book. It treats current technological and ecological crises as one condition.

Braidotti starts from contemporary contradictions: care robots, digital waste, synthetic biology and the climate crisis. She argues these must be considered together and calls the result a posthuman convergence. The text criticizes humanism and anthropocentrism. It turns to how knowledge is produced and how academic structures shape it, and asks for imagination, endurance, connectivity and perspectives that are embodied and grounded in the only world we have. It was delivered at Harvard's Graduate School of Design in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on 12 March 2019, with an introduction by John May.

The book is part of The Incidents, a series from Harvard Design Press and Sternberg Press edited by Ken Stewart and Marielle Suba. It is 80 pages in a small softcover format, designed by ELLA with Gabrielle Pulgar and published in December 2024.
tags: Media Theory, Posthumanism, Critical Theory, Philosophy, Design Studies

title: Memesthetics: The Eternal September of Art
description:
A history of the internet meme told through its relation to art, tracing a path the publisher describes as running from Duchamp to TikTok.

Tanni examines how internet memes, GIFs, photoshopping and social media practices connect to the historical avant-garde and to modernist and postmodernist art theory. She also considers how digital culture has changed traditional art institutions. NERO presents it as the first book to draw a comprehensive map of the relationship between the visual arts and digital culture since the early 2000s. The English edition, 268 pages in an 11 × 17 cm format, appeared in 2024.

Valentina Tanni is an art historian and curator who works where art and technology meet, and who teaches digital art and internet culture studies at institutions in Milan and Rome. The book was first published in Italian as Memestetica, with a second Italian edition issued later.
tags: Media Theory, Internet Culture, Memes, Digital Art, Visual Culture, Art History
notes: English edition. First published in Italian as Memestetica (NERO), with a second Italian edition. Identified from a spine photograph; edition not checked against the copy.

title: The Medium Is the Massage: An Inventory of Effects
description:
A visual essay on how successive media reshape the environment in which people think and live, set as a sequence of pages where text and image carry equal weight.

The book was produced by Jerome Agel and first published in New York by Random House in 1967, with Bantam issuing a paperback the same year. It combines McLuhan's statements on technology and culture with about one hundred black-and-white illustrations arranged by Quentin Fiore, and it asks readers to attend to the effects of a medium rather than its content. The Gingko Press softcover in a small 4 × 7 inch format reprints it at 160 pages, and the publisher calls it McLuhan's most popular book, perhaps as influential as Understanding Media.

Marshall McLuhan (1911 to 1980) also wrote Understanding Media. Quentin Fiore is credited as co-author, and Jerome Agel as producer.
